Then find what changed between them: a deploy, the data, or the configuration. Next, responding.

To finish the chapter, put the pieces together into an incident. At six the freshness check fails: refunds are missing from the third of March. Triage comes first: what is affected, who owns it, and how far back the damage goes, using the interval list from chapter seven. Then contain it. Pause the finance report DAG, so the wrong figures do not flow on into the margin report. Pausing a DAG is almost always safe: it stops new runs and changes nothing that exists. Then repair, by clearing the affected tasks with a narrow scope that you have checked, which is only safe because those tasks are idempotent. Then verify, by reconciling the data against the source, because green task states after a repair prove only that tasks ran. Some interventions deserve more caution. Setting a pool to zero slots is a good way to protect an external system that is struggling. Marking a task as successful by hand is only acceptable when the data has been verified, since it tells every downstream task that the input is good. And editing tables directly should be rare, recorded and reviewed. Finally, write it up. Next chapter: the whole system.

The last chapter steps back to look at the whole system. Here is the order pipeline as the course has built it. It waits for the partner's refunds, extracts the day's orders, stages them, builds the sales tables, checks them, and publishes the summary. The table beside it is the more important half, because each step carries a protection from an earlier chapter. The interval timetable gives every run a data interval, and every path and partition comes from that interval, never from the clock. The refunds wait is deferred, so it holds no worker, and it has a timeout, so it fails visibly. Extraction fans out per shop, bounded by a pool and by batching. Staging replaces exactly one day. The Spark build has a stable name, so a retry finds the job instead of starting another. The quality gate reconciles totals against the source and fails closed. And publication is an atomic swap that emits an asset event carrying the day. Even so, the design needs two things that live outside the DAG: a freshness check from outside the pipeline, owned by a person, and a recovery plan, tested before it is needed. Next, the engines it coordinates.

In this pipeline, Airflow does not transform a single row itself. The heavy work runs in the warehouse, in dbt and on Spark, and Airflow coordinates them. The useful thing to notice is that the contract is the same with every engine. Airflow passes the run's identity in: the day and the run id, as query parameters, dbt variables or job arguments, never pasted into command text. And it gets something back: a status, a job or query id, and a few counts worth checking. A failure inside the engine should become a failed task, with the engine's own id in the task log, so a person can follow it across. In practice, warehouse SQL runs through the SQL execute query operator with bound parameters. dbt runs through a dbt build command, or one of the integrations that turn a dbt project into tasks, with the day passed as a variable. Spark runs through a provider operator for your platform, with a stable job name, as in chapter four. What stays out of this course is the inside of each engine: SQL design, dbt modelling and Spark tuning each have their own courses. Next, where to cut DAGs.

As more teams come to depend on the pipeline, one DAG tends to become several, and the question is where to cut. Good boundaries follow ownership. Here, the data platform team owns ingestion, analytics engineering owns the daily sales build, and finance data owns the finance report: three DAGs, each with one owner who is paged when it breaks. Cadence is another natural boundary. If orders are ingested every hour but sales are built daily, those are different schedules, and one DAG would have to pretend otherwise. And when many consumers need the same output, publish it as an asset rather than having each consumer reach into the producer's tasks. The asset between teams needs a contract, though, because an asset event alone only says updated. Write down the owner who is paged on a breach. The grain, one row per day and shop, and the freshness promise, yesterday by six. The event's extra field, so consumers know which day an update covers. And how changes are handled: announced ahead of time, so the finance team is not the first to discover a new column. Next, planning for outages.

Recovery plans are best written before the outage, and every one of them has a limit worth saying out loud. If the warehouse is down for six hours, tasks retry and then fail, and a backfill repairs the gap, but the backfill itself must be paced so that it does not swamp the warehouse the moment it returns. If a worker is lost in the middle of a Spark job, the next attempt can recover it, but only if the job has a stable name to look up. If raw input files have expired, no orchestration can help: a replay needs its inputs. The subtle one is restoring the metadata database. Suppose it is restored from a two o'clock backup after a failure at five. Airflow now has no record of anything that happened between two and five. Those runs are forgotten, the scheduler sees gaps, and work runs again. Idempotent tasks make that safe; anything that appends or sends will duplicate. Asset events from those hours are gone, so consumers that were waiting for them may never start. So after a restore, reconcile the outputs against the data itself, not against Airflow's states. Next, upgrades.

Airflow versions move on, and so do providers, so plan upgrades as ordinary changes with a test path and a rollback plan. An upgrade changes more than code: the scheduler, the API, often the providers, and the schema of the metadata database. Start by reading the release notes and, for a major version, the migration guide, looking for breaking changes. Lint the DAG code: the ruff linter includes rules, prefixed AIR, that flag Airflow 2 imports and patterns that changed in Airflow 3. Upgrade staging first, ideally with a copy of production's metadata, so the database migration itself is tested on realistic data. Then run the integrity and integration tests from chapter nine against the new versions. Rollback deserves honesty. The image is easy: redeploy the old one. The metadata schema is not. Database migrations are not always reversible, so the reliable way back is to restore the backup taken just before running the migration. And anything that ran between the upgrade and the rollback then needs reconciling, exactly like the restore in the previous section. Next, the final question.

The course ends with the question it began with: what is Airflow for? It fits bounded work, in runs that end, with real dependencies between steps and between systems, where history matters: retries, data intervals, backfills, and a record of what ran and when. Our order pipeline has all of those, which is why it fits. Other workloads fit other tools, and choosing them is not a failure. One script, once a night, with no dependencies, is well served by cron. Transformations that live entirely inside one warehouse may be best expressed in dbt, perhaps triggered by Airflow, perhaps not. Continuous events that need low latency belong in a stream processor, and a request that needs an answer now belongs in a service. So ask four questions. Is the work bounded? Are there real dependencies? Will you need to replay history by interval? And who will operate it, at what cost? From here, try the ideas on a different workload, compare its scheduling and side-effect contracts with this one, and check the current documentation, and your recovery evidence, before operating a real deployment.
